extracted.intended_audience: comics scholars, cartoonists, editors, designers, and students of graphic narrative
extracted.subtask_description: Analytical rubric for evaluating and designing comic-page layouts (the "mise en page") that relates panel composition to narrative function, across single pages and book-objects. Focuses on four conceptions (conventional, decorative, rhetorical, productive) and the design/production choices that affect readability and overall work coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative–Composition relation (two axes)
rubrics_metrics.description: A combinatory chart taking account of the two components of the comic strip (narrative vs composition) and of the types of relation which can be established between them (autonomy vs interdependence) to distinguish four general modes of page and panel utilization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this two-axis framework (narrative ↔ composition; autonomy ↔ interdependence) as the basic analytic dimension: it yields the four modes—Conventional, Decorative, Rhetorical, Productive. The classification is analytical, not historical; borders are fuzzy and a single work or page may instantiate multiple positions. Judge according to particular work; recurrence of arrangements helps decide which conception is in play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventional utilization (regular grid / 'waffle iron')
rubrics_metrics.description: A strongly codified system in which the arrangement of panels repeats (often lines of equal height, e.g., four tiers) so that the framework becomes transparent; originated in constraints of daily-strip publication and facilitates recomposition into strips/columns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characteristics: regular rows/columns, easy left-to-right/top-to-bottom reading, reproducible for serial publication. Advantages: small changes in gesture/expression gain significance because of constancy; efficient for continuity and serial narratives; resilient to reassembly. Example authors: Buck Danny, Schulz, Franquin. Note: pushing the constancy to extremes can become 'productive' rather than merely conventional. Beware of reformatting (e.g., pocket reprints) that can devastate page unity except in conventional layouts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decorative utilization (page as independent aesthetic object)
rubrics_metrics.description: The page is considered an independent unit whose aesthetic organization trumps narrative concerns; each page often designed in advance and strives to differ from others (will to surprise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characteristics: tabular/painterly approach, emphasis on symmetry, lines, balances, and purely aesthetic devices (inset panels, border violations) often serve decoration more than sequence. Examples: Edgar P. Jacobs, Philippe Druillet, Burne Hogarth. Anti-patterns: decorative effects that act as compensations for sequential poverty or degrade sequential continuity; facile aestheticism that doesn’t exploit medium-specific possibilities. Evaluate whether aesthetic choices meaningfully serve the work or merely ornament it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical utilization (page serving a pre-existing narrative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Panels and the page are subordinated to a narrative; size, distribution, pace, and placement of images are used methodically to support and accentuate the narration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characteristics: panel dimensions conform to action, placement (top/bottom/left/right) modulates effect, large panels emphasize powerful moments or complex scenes. Examples: Hergé (Tintin) where panel sizes are chosen to support specific actions; Sokal’s use of horizontal/vertical panels to control pace; Will Eisner’s borderless sequences that still preserve narrative clarity. Consider conflicts with other requirements (e.g., rhythm) and the effect of reformatting on rhetorical unity. Favor choices that underline contents rather than ornament them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Productive utilization (page dictates/generates narrative)
rubrics_metrics.description: A page organization that seems to dictate the narrative: a particular arrangement generates a piece of narration (the narrative is a consequence of the page figure rather than its pretext).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characteristics: the layout produces events, movements, or transformations (e.g., characters expanding or shrinking to fit panels), adjacency-driven reading paths, destabilization of linear reading. Examples: Winsor McCay (Little Nemo), Fred, Régis Franc. Productive use is easier on a single-page scale than across an entire album; to be viable over many pages it must be combined with rhetorical devices or governed by a system of rules to avoid mere aestheticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel size and placement as narrative tools
rubrics_metrics.description: The dimension and placement of individual panels are deliberate rhetorical devices: verticality, horizontality, and scale can slow/speed pace, emphasize action, or change psychological effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use panel dimensions and their placement consciously: vertical panels for nervous dialogue or intensity, horizontal sequences to slow pace, half-page or large images to emphasize complex or powerful moments. Placement on a right- or left-hand page or at top/bottom affects discovery and revelation (e.g., corner placement to preserve a revelation on the following double page). Evaluate whether sizes/placements accentuate narrative goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regularity and repetition to amplify small changes
rubrics_metrics.description: A constant repeated grid (the 'waffle iron') can make minimal modifications in gesture or expression acquire considerable significance because of the stable frame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ regular frameworks when you want micro-variations to carry weight; good for sequences where immobility or slight shifts are narratively meaningful. Examples: Pratt’s Tango, sequences by Schulz or Franquin. Recognize when radicalizing the grid turns it into productive layout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Premeditated/design-in-advance page composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Many decorative pages are designed in advance with too-perfect relations of lines and symmetry to be accidental; the page as a planned concrete object whose harmony is paramount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When planning pages, consider preliminary design of lines, balances, and symmetries. This supports aesthetic coherence but must be evaluated for how it integrates (or not) with narrative function. Distinguish genuine integration from mere stylistic display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inset panels and border violations (effects vs continuity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inset panels and violations of panel borders are spectacular effects often used in decorative layouts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These devices can produce striking visuals but frequently function as degradations of sequential continuity or compensations for limited narrative invention. Use them when they serve a narrative or produce meaningful formal effects; avoid gratuitous use that interrupts sequential logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve narrative clarity amid stylistic freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental visual devices (absence of contours, undulating connective lines, suppression of caption boxes) may create associative or memory effects but should not damage narrative clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Will Eisner’s borderless sequences support memory/association while keeping clarity via prominent characters guiding the gaze. Reward experiments that maintain intelligibility; penalize formal choices that obscure essential narrative trajectories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading path complexity and crossed readings (multi-plane narration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pages can present multiple narrative planes or parallel montages that create ambiguous or crossing reading trajectories (e.g., oscillation between reading orders A-B-C vs plane-by-plane traversal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and map possible reading routes; consider whether the intended oscillation (read-and-reread) enriches meaning or merely confuses. Example: Régis Franc’s multi-level strips where reading forces constant back-and-forth; the reader may need to alternate orders to capture story and effects. Evaluate usability and intended effect: deliberate destabilization can be a valid aesthetic goal if it is coherent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale and publication/format constraints (serial vs album)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication formats (daily strips, album page counts, format sizes) impose constraints that shape mise en page choices; standard editorial molds (e.g., 48-page A4 albums vs 64-page Tintin model) have long-term narrative effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design with production contexts in mind: strips must recombine into pages; reformatting (e.g., recoloring/remontage, pocket reprints, translation editions that change dimensions or break up issues) can irreparably damage page unity and narrative coherence. Editors/translators should respect original pagination/scale to preserve structural games (e.g., Watchmen's design rhythms). When possible, choose formats adapted to the project rather than imposed standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book-object coherence and paratextual design as integral to narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Cover, title pages, recurring motifs, simulated paratexts (ads, letters), and format variations can be integral to the project and contribute to meaning across the volume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the book as a total object: recurring motifs across covers/title pages (Watchmen), multiple formats within a series (Chris Ware’s Acme Novelty Library), and tight integration of design elements can enrich narrative. Editors and authors should coordinate design, lettering, coloring, and mock paratexts as narrative parameters; avoid standardizing a carefully designed work to fit conventional editorial standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color, black-and-white, and pagination as rhetorical choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Choices like color vs B&W, page count, and whether the number of pages varies according to story needs are rhetorical/editorial decisions that affect narrative presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these parameters to align book form with project aims (e.g., Tintin’s variable page counts in early black-and-white albums; Spiegelman’s alignment with literary presentation). Evaluate whether the medium choices serve the story’s tone, pacing, and reader expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid spectacle-for-its-own-sake (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectacular graphic upheavals or flashy special effects that prioritize shock/value over narrative function quickly wear thin and may not renew the relation to narration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat spectacular devices skeptically unless they contribute to deeper narrative or formal aims. The flashy can age quickly; prioritize meaningful invention over transient visual novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixing modes and contextual judgement (categories as tools, not laws)
rubrics_metrics.description: The four uses (conventional, decorative, rhetorical, productive) are analytical tools; pages and albums may combine modes and shift instantly from one operation to another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rigidly classify works; examine recurrence of arrangements to identify dominant modes. Evaluate pages in context—the same author or album may employ multiple conceptions; a viable long-form project often balances productive and rhetorical uses to generate a sustained, medium-specific fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Productive mode requires governing rules to scale beyond a few pages
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic that constantly redefines page formats needs a system of rules so variations have meaning beyond mere aestheticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a work changes the format of pages frequently, provide an internal logic or system so that variations contribute narratively rather than merely ornamentally. Example: Martin Vaughn-James’s La Cage as exemplary; without rules, variations risk being arbitrary. For serial or long-form projects, combine productive devices with stable rhetorical elements to maintain continuity.
